chapters.title: Build a rule
chapters.question: Can you make a network behave the way you intend?

scenes.title: Two inputs. One result.
text: Toggle Request and Permission independently. The result of this network depends on both values, not on the order in which you pressed the buttons. ON and OFF are names for Boolean states here. They are not voltage measurements or proof that a real system has checked anyone’s identity.

Inspect the AND component and follow the connected lines. Each line shows the current value produced by its source. Text labels accompany the visual emphasis so that the explanation does not depend only on color. Try all four possible pairs of input values before deciding what rule the gate implements.

scenes.title: Make the rule explicit.
text: A truth table is a complete list of outcomes for a finite set of input combinations. For two Boolean inputs there are four combinations. Describing only the case where both inputs are ON leaves most of the rule unstated, even if that is the case you first expected to matter.

Use the process panel to organize your investigation, then return to the network when useful. The goal is a rule you can explain and reproduce. Merely watching a highlighted line is not enough if you cannot say which change would make that line switch off.

scenes.title: Change AND into OR.
text: This network contains the same two independent inputs and a different combining rule. Turn one input ON while leaving the other OFF, then compare the result with the first network. A change to one gate can change the overall behavior while the visual arrangement stays familiar.

The OR rule here is inclusive: having both inputs ON does not cancel the result. Words such as either can be ambiguous in everyday conversation, so the workbench gives you exact input combinations to inspect. Distinguish the rule being demonstrated from a story someone tells about what the input labels mean.

scenes.title: Reason about a pathway.
text: Connected gates let you work from local rules towards an overall result. You can trace forward from a changed input, or reason backwards from an output condition. The network in this lesson has no feedback loops, so every value can be resolved from earlier values.

That restriction is part of the model. Real digital systems can have memory and timing, but drawing a loop in this particular workbench would require a definition of those behaviors. A useful lesson engine should reject unsupported structure rather than quietly display an arbitrary answer for it.

scenes.title: Add a condition that must be absent.
scenes.deck: Add a condition that must be absent.
text: The second input now represents a block. A NOT gate reverses that input before it reaches AND. Try a request with no block, then keep the request ON and introduce the block. The visible connections let you identify the exact place where the change reverses the final outcome.

This is an illustrative policy, not a real access-control implementation. Its value is the logical structure: Request AND NOT Blocked. You can use the same small vocabulary to express other conditions, provided you define what the values mean and avoid importing real-world guarantees that the diagram does not establish.

scenes.title: A decision can be inspected.
text: You have compared three networks without changing the way you operate the workbench. Each network is data: nodes, connections, initial input values and explanations. The renderer and evaluator apply the same supported rules to every example.

That separation also makes the explanation testable. An invalid connection or a cycle should be caught before a learner sees the lesson. Correct logical evaluation is still only one layer of correctness: the labels and the intended real-world application must also be examined. Keep both layers in mind when following a more complicated system.

scenes.title: Exactly one. Not both.
text: Start by testing the supplied network. It connects A and B to Either, an OR gate, and sends that result straight to the output. That works when exactly one input is ON. It also turns ON when both inputs are ON, which breaks the new goal. The test table checks every combination and gives you a concrete case to repair.

Use the connection controls or drag between ports to rewire the supplied components. Remove a wire before replacing its destination input. Both and Combine are separate AND gates; Invert supplies NOT. Spare gates may remain disconnected. The test cares about the complete input-to-output behavior, so swapping equivalent AND inputs does not make a correct solution wrong. A missing connection on the route to Result produces an incomplete draft, never a fabricated OFF.

scenes.title: A request with a blocker.
text: Begin with an empty workbench and make a different rule. Read A as a request and B as a blocker. The output should be ON only when the request is present and the blocker is absent. Predict the four outcomes before wiring. This is a Boolean exercise, not a real authentication system or a promise that a request has been authorized.

Test a complete design and inspect its input combinations. If one fails, trace the input values through your gates and compare the observed result with your intention. Editing clears the previous test result, because that result belongs to the old wiring. Your draft and input choices survive a local reload, while test feedback is recomputed only when requested. Reset returns to the supplied starting point. You can investigate and repair a design without receiving a score or following one required wiring diagram.

nodes.label: Request
nodes.explanation: This is one independent input. Toggle it and follow the changed connections. ON represents Boolean true; OFF represents false.

nodes.label: Permission
nodes.explanation: This is another independent input. A gate combines its value with the request according to a stated rule.

nodes.label: AND
nodes.explanation: AND is ON only when every incoming value is ON. Try each of the four possible input combinations.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.explanation: The output copies the last gate. It tells you the result of this particular network, not whether a real action is safe or appropriate.

nodes.label: Request
nodes.explanation: This is one independent input. Toggle it and follow the changed connections. ON represents Boolean true; OFF represents false.

nodes.label: Blocked
nodes.explanation: ON means an explicit block is present. Notice how the NOT gate reverses this value before it reaches AND.

nodes.label: NOT
nodes.explanation: NOT reverses its single input. A missing block becomes permission to continue; a present block removes that permission.

nodes.label: AND
nodes.explanation: The request can continue only if Request is ON and the inverted Blocked signal is ON.

nodes.label: Result
nodes.explanation: The output copies the last gate. It tells you the result of this particular network, not whether a real action is safe or appropriate.

construction.goal: Make Result ON when exactly one of A and B is ON. Both OFF and both ON must give OFF.
construction.hint: Compare “at least one” with “both.” An inverter can remove the both-ON case before the final combination.

nodes.label: Either
nodes.explanation: OR is ON when at least one of its two inputs is ON.

nodes.label: Both
nodes.explanation: AND is ON only when both of its inputs are ON.

nodes.label: Invert
nodes.explanation: NOT reverses its one input: ON becomes OFF and OFF becomes ON.

nodes.label: Combine
nodes.explanation: This second AND gate can combine the results of other components.

construction.goal: Make Result ON only when A is ON and B is OFF. Treat A as a request and B as a blocker.
construction.hint: The blocker’s permission condition is the opposite of B. Combine that with the request.
